description: How to describe how your code slows down as data grows — and answer the most-asked interview question.

screens.body: Big O is a way to describe how slow your code gets as your data gets bigger. Not how many seconds it takes — how the work GROWS. If doubling your data doubles the work, that's O(n). If doubling your data quadruples the work, that's O(n²).
screens.heading: Big O in 30 seconds
screens.keyPoint: Big O describes growth, not speed.

check.question: What does Big O describe?
options: How many seconds the code takes on your laptop
How the work grows as the data gets bigger
How pretty the variable names are

screens.body: O(1) means the work stays the same no matter how big your data is. Grabbing an item from an array by its index is O(1) — it's one step whether the array has 10 items or 10 million.

code.snippet: const first = users[0]; // one step, always

screens.heading: O(1) — constant time

check.question: Grabbing users[0] from an array is which Big O?

screens.body: O(n) means the work grows step-for-step with your data. One loop over an array of n items does n steps of work. Twice the items, twice the work. Most simple loops are O(n).
screens.heading: O(n) — linear time
screens.keyPoint: One loop over n items = O(n).

check.question: One loop over n items is usually:

screens.body: A loop inside a loop. For each of the n items, you do n more steps of work. That's n × n = n² steps. This gets slow FAST — 1,000 items means 1,000,000 steps. If an interviewer spots this in your code, they'll ask how you'd fix it.
screens.heading: O(n²) — quadratic time
screens.keyPoint: Nested loops over the same data = O(n²). Watch out.

check.question: A loop inside a loop, both over n, is:

screens.body: O(log n) means you throw away half the data with every step. Binary search works like this: check the middle, discard the half that can't contain your answer, repeat. Even with a million items, you only need about 20 steps.

code.snippet:
// binary search: pick the middle, discard half, repeat
// 1,000,000 items → ~20 steps

screens.heading: O(log n) — logarithmic time
screens.keyPoint: Halving the problem each step = O(log n). Very fast.

check.question: Binary search is fast because each step:
options: Throws away about half the remaining data

screens.body: Three steps. 1) Count the loops — each loop over n multiplies the work by n. 2) Drop the constants — O(2n) is just O(n); at scale, the 2 doesn't matter. 3) Keep only the biggest term — O(n² + n) is just O(n²); the n² drowns out everything else.
screens.heading: How to figure it out
screens.keyPoint: Count loops, drop constants, keep the biggest term.

check.question: When you simplify Big O, you should:
options: Drop constants and keep the biggest term
Always call it O(n²) to be safe

screens.body: "What's the time complexity of your code?" is one of the most-asked interview questions there is. Now you have the framework: walk through your loops, name the Big O, and if it's O(n²), say how you'd improve it. That's the whole game — and it's exactly what your SwiftGigs code walkthrough needs too.
screens.heading: Why interviews love this
screens.keyPoint: Name your loops, name your Big O.

check.question: If your code is O(n²), a strong interview move is to:
options: Name the Big O and say how you would improve it
